title: Government plans Tk 300 crore plant to make animal vaccines at home
excerpt: Bangladesh makes only about 12% of the 260 crore doses its livestock and poultry need each year and imports the rest for about Tk 5,000 crore.

image.alt: Cattle at a village homestead in Dinajpur district

content:
The government is preparing to build an animal vaccine plant costing about Tk 300 crore (about US$25 million) to cut imports, The Daily Star reported on Friday, 13 November, citing Department of Livestock Services (DLS) documents and officials.

The plan

  • First step: a feasibility study, planned for 1 October 2026 to 31 March 2027, on demand, design, equipment and costs.
  • Site: about 200 acres identified in Gabtali, Bogura.
  • Status: the Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock has given approval in principle, but the project is not yet in the Annual Development Programme (ADP), so no money has been released.

The gap

  • Need: about 260 crore (2.6 billion) doses a year for some 46.5 crore livestock and poultry, according to DLS data.
  • Made at home: 32 crore doses a year at the Bangladesh Livestock Research Institute (BLRI) in Savar, or 12.31% of the need. A DLS unit in Cumilla makes a small amount more. Both facilities are about 30 years old.
  • Imports: the rest, from 18 countries, at an estimated Tk 5,000 crore a year.
  • Foot-and-mouth disease: demand of about 3.5 crore doses a year against domestic production of 20 lakh to 26 lakh.
  • Fowl cholera: demand of 22.4 crore doses against 1.6 crore made locally.

What officials said

Md Shahzaman Khan, director general of the DLS, said the plan follows the government's election pledge to reduce import dependence through local production and public-private partnerships, according to the newspaper. Prof Hafiza Khatun, head of animal science at Bangladesh Agricultural University, welcomed the plan but said "proper management and biosecurity measures are essential to preventing disease outbreaks and improving productivity", and called for more direct support to farmers.

Why it matters

Cattle, goats and poultry are a main source of income for poor rural households, and many NGO and microfinance livelihood programmes rely on them. Vaccine shortages and outbreaks can wipe out those assets. NGOs that train community animal health workers or run livestock projects have a stake in whether local supply grows and reaches villages at an affordable price.

What to watch

Whether the feasibility study gets money in the revised ADP, and when its findings are published.

Sources

  • Govt eyes Tk 300cr plant to cut animal vaccine imports, The Daily Star, 13 November 2026
